lesson.title: God, Gold, and Glory: Why Europe Looked Across the Atlantic
lesson.summary: This section explains the economic, religious, and political motives, along with new maritime technologies, that drove Portugal, Spain, and other European kingdoms to launch overseas voyages of exploration in the fifteenth century.
lesson.body:
By the middle of the fifteenth century, European kingdoms had strong incentives to find new routes to the wealth of Asia. For centuries, spices, silk, and other luxury goods had reached Europe through long overland and sea routes controlled by Muslim and Italian merchants, passing through the Middle East and the eastern Mediterranean. When the Ottoman Empire captured Constantinople in 1453, gaining firm control over key trade routes linking Europe to Asia, European merchants and monarchs faced even higher costs and greater uncertainty in accessing eastern goods. Finding an alternative route, one that bypassed these middlemen entirely, promised enormous profit to whichever kingdom achieved it first.

Portugal took the early lead. Prince Henry, later remembered as Henry the Navigator, sponsored decades of voyages down the west coast of Africa beginning in the 1420s, gradually pushing Portuguese knowledge of Atlantic winds, currents, and coastlines further south. This investment paid off when Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa in 1488, and again when Vasco da Gama completed a sea route to India in 1498, opening direct maritime trade with Asia and making Portugal, briefly, one of the wealthiest and most strategically positioned kingdoms in Europe. Spain, watching its neighbor's success, had its own reasons to seek an alternative approach, and in 1492, the same year the centuries long Reconquista ended with the fall of Granada, the last Muslim controlled kingdom in Iberia, the Spanish crown funded Christopher Columbus's westward voyage in the hope of reaching Asia by sailing in the opposite direction.

Economic motives were only part of the story. European monarchs and the Catholic Church saw overseas expansion as an opportunity to spread Christianity to new populations, a goal that took on particular urgency in Spain and Portugal, both freshly emerged from centuries of religious conflict with Muslim states on the Iberian Peninsula. Missionaries frequently accompanied or followed early explorers, and religious conversion, whether pursued sincerely or used to justify conquest and forced labor, became a consistent feature of European colonization efforts. Political rivalry mattered as well. Portugal, Spain, and later France, England, and the Netherlands were competing, ambitious states, and the prestige, resources, and strategic advantage that came with new territories and trade routes were valuable in their own right, independent of any single voyage's profits.

None of this exploration would have been possible without real advances in maritime technology. The caravel, a smaller, more maneuverable ship developed by the Portuguese, could sail more effectively against the wind than earlier vessels. Navigational tools including the magnetic compass and the astrolabe, along with steadily improving maps and accumulated knowledge of Atlantic wind patterns, allowed sailors to venture farther from familiar coastlines with greater confidence of finding their way back.

Together, these economic, religious, political, and technological factors explain why the late fifteenth century became a turning point. The chapters that follow trace how these motives played out in practice, beginning with Columbus's 1492 voyage and continuing through the Spanish, French, and Dutch exploration and colonization efforts that reshaped the Americas in the centuries that followed.
